Getting started

1. What administrators do

SutraFlow has two kinds of people. Designers build Sutras in the studio and release them; the SutraFlow User Guide is theirs. Administrators install and upgrade SutraFlow, run its engines, look after its database, people and security, and receive releases on test and production servers. This guide is theirs.

TaskWhere
Choose a set-up: one server, PostgreSQL, a cluster, DockerPlanning a server
Install a server, by pages in the browser or silently from a fileThe web installer, Silent installation
Upgrade it, with a backup and a way backUpgrading
Start, stop and configure itThe sutraflow command and server settings
Engines, clusters and sizingRunning in production, Setting up a cluster, Sizing
Deployed Sutras, runs, alerts, the gateway, people and the audit logThe Admin Console
Releases on test and production serversReceiving releases
Health, metrics, traces and logsMonitoring

Designers who also run their own development machine need only The web installer and Development machines.

Who is an administrator

An account with the Administrator role on all projects. The installer makes the first one; more are added under Admin Console, Users. Some tasks need only part of it: the Engines, Gateway, Users and roles, Audit and Server settings permissions are separate, so an operations team can run the servers without designing anything.

2. Planning a server

SutraFlow is one Node.js program. It needs Node.js 22.13 or later (24 recommended) and nothing else: its own data starts in SQLite, built into Node. Everything else is a choice.

Which set-up

Set-upDatabaseGood for
One studioSQLite in the data folderA developer machine, a proof of concept, a small server: about 420 small steps a second, nothing to install
A studio and an engine beside itSQLite or PostgreSQLMore work on one machine, and one keeps serving while the other restarts
A cluster: engines on several machinesPostgreSQL (14 or later, with pgvector for knowledge bases)Failover, more throughput, production apart from design
DockerPostgreSQL in the cluster fileContainers and Kubernetes; one engine per container

The installer asks for each of these. Moving from SQLite to PostgreSQL later takes a minute (Moving to PostgreSQL), so starting small is safe.

Do I need a web server (Apache, IIS, nginx, Laragon, WAMP, LAMP)?

No. SutraFlow has web servers of its own: the studio port serves the designer, Admin Console, Approval Center, the guides and the admin API; the gateway ports serve the deployed Sutras (REST, SOAP, WebSocket, MCP, AI agents) over HTTP and HTTPS, with certificates of your own or from Let's Encrypt, renewed automatically. It needs no PHP and no Apache. Laragon, WAMP or LAMP are only a convenient way to get Node.js, PostgreSQL and MySQL on one machine (Development machines).

Put a web server or load balancer in front of SutraFlow (a reverse proxy) only when one of these applies:

WhenWhy a web server in front helps
Ports 80 and 443 are already used by Apache, IIS or nginx on the machineOnly one program can listen on a port: the existing web server keeps them and passes SutraFlow's addresses (a host name or a path) on to its ports.
Several gateway engines should answer at one addressA load balancer spreads callers over the engines and stops sending to one that is down (health check /ready); see Running in production.
Your organisation requires a central proxy, web application firewall or single TLS entry pointCertificates, logging, IP rules and firewalls stay where the organisation manages them.
A friendly local address on a developer machine, such as http://sutra.testLaragon's Apache gives every project a .test name; SutraFlow keeps its own port behind it.
The studio must be reached from other machinesThe studio listens on 127.0.0.1 by default. A proxy with its own access rules (VPN, single sign-on, IP allow list) is safer than opening the admin port directly.

Otherwise leave it out: a proxy is one more thing to configure, secure and keep running, and SutraFlow's gateway already handles TLS, Let's Encrypt, security policies, rate limits and request size limits itself. When you do use one:

  • Forward to the gateway's HTTPS port (8443), not its HTTP port: SutraFlow treats a call as HTTPS only when it reaches its own HTTPS port, and security policies have Require HTTPS on by default, so calls forwarded over plain HTTP are refused (403). Turn Require HTTPS off on a policy only when the link from the proxy to SutraFlow is private.
  • Callers' addresses: SutraFlow sees the proxy's address, not the caller's (it does not read X-Forwarded-For), so IP rules and per-address rate limits apply to the proxy; keep those in the proxy, or use API keys, tokens or gateway apps to tell callers apart.
  • Pass /.well-known/acme-challenge/ through unchanged if SutraFlow renews its own certificates, keep long-running requests open (AI agents and approvals can take minutes), and allow WebSocket upgrades.

A release unpacked in a web folder

Every release carries an .htaccess (Apache) and a web.config (IIS) that refuse everything in the folder except one page, install-sutraflow.html. Unpacked under a web root (Laragon's www, htdocs, wwwroot), the web server never serves sutraflow.env, the data folder or the keys; opening the folder in a browser shows that page, which says how to install and start SutraFlow. An upgrade keeps a site's own .htaccess and web.config, and adds the release's when there is none.

Guidelines

Keep the studio on 127.0.0.1: port 4800 is for your team (designer, Admin Console, admin API). Everything others call goes through the gateway ports.
Back up the data folder, and above all data/master.key: without it the encrypted secrets cannot be read (Where SutraFlow keeps its data).

Installing and upgrading

3. The web installer

Each release comes as sutraflow-<version>-windows.zip and sutraflow-<version>-linux.tar.gz, already built, each with a .sha256 file; the -offline archives have the runtime packages inside, for servers without access to the npm registry.

  1. Check the download: sha256sum -c sutraflow-VERSION-linux.tar.gz.sha256, or on Windows Get-FileHash sutraflow-VERSION-windows.zip -Algorithm SHA256 against the .sha256 file.
  2. Unpack it into an empty folder: tar -xzf sutraflow-VERSION-linux.tar.gz -C /opt, or on Windows with Explorer or 7-Zip into C:\SutraFlow.
  3. In that folder run bin/sutraflow install (Windows: bin\sutraflow.cmd install).

The installer starts on this machine only, at 127.0.0.1 on a free port from 4790, with a one-time address that it opens in the browser (--no-open prints it instead; --port chooses the port). Nobody else, and no other web page in the browser, can drive it. Nothing changes until you choose Install on the Review page.

Welcome

The system check: Node.js version, a folder it can write, the runtime packages and free disk space. A missing requirement stops it here with what to do. Choose Install for a new SutraFlow in this folder, or Upgrade to bring another installation up to this version (Upgrading).

Administrator

The first account, which manages users, roles, projects and the server: user name, optional email, and a password of at least 12 characters with upper and lower case letters and digits, typed twice. It is not made when the database already holds accounts.

Database

  • SQLite: a file in the data folder, sutra.db or a name you give. Nothing to install. SQLite has no user names or passwords: the file is protected by the data folder's permissions, and SutraFlow's vault encrypts the secrets inside it with data/master.key.
  • PostgreSQL: host, port, database, user, password and SSL (off on this machine or a trusted network, require to encrypt, verify to also check the certificate, for hosted PostgreSQL). Create it when missing makes the database when the user may (CREATEDB). pgvector is required by default: Test connection enables it in the database when it is installed on the server, or says how to install it; choose Continue without pgvector only when no knowledge base will be kept in PostgreSQL. Next stays closed until the test passes. The password is kept in sutraflow.env as SUTRA_DB_PASSWORD, readable by this server's account only, apart from the address.

Server

Where SutraFlow listens: 127.0.0.1 (this machine, recommended; put a proxy in front to reach it from elsewhere) or 0.0.0.0; the environment (development, test or production: a production server takes Sutras only from releases); the studio port (4800) and the gateway ports (8080 and 8443). A headless engine beside it adds a second process on the same database, with its own ports. Check ports tests each one; a busy port gets a free one suggested, and Use the free ports takes them.

Node memory: each engine is its own Node.js process with its own memory. 0 lets Node.js decide; the page shows this machine's memory and a suggested size, and Use N MB takes it. It can be changed later in the Admin Console (Engines, Tuning) and applies at a restart.

Cluster

The engines that share the work through one database. The cluster name is shown in the Admin Console. Each engine has a name (this server's and the one beside it are filled in from the computer name) and May lead: the leader runs timers, listeners, recovery and housekeeping, and is elected among the engines that may lead; another takes over when it stops. Allowing only one fixes the leader, without failover, and the page says so. With PostgreSQL, Add an engine on another machine adds engines with their own ports and memory; each gets a settings file to copy to its machine. Names, the cluster name and who may lead are changed later in Admin Console, Engines.

Review

Everything once more. Save answers as a config file (2.1.2) writes sutraflow-install.json: the same choices for a silent install of the next server (Silent installation). Its passwords are environment variables to set there, never the passwords themselves. Start SutraFlow when installed starts the studio, and the engine beside it when there is one.

Install and Done

Each step with its result: settings file, data folder, tables and the administrator, the admin token, and the start. When it is done the page gives the address to sign in at, a settings file for each further engine, and the installer's log (also kept in data/logs/installer.log; 2.1.2). The installer then locks itself (data/install.lock), so it cannot be run over a working installation; sutraflow install --reset removes the lock.

After installing

Keep data/master.key safe and backed up: it unlocks the vault.
Start SutraFlow with the machine: sutraflow service prints a Windows scheduled task or a Linux systemd unit.
Sign in to the Admin Console and add the people who will use it (Users).

4. Silent installation

For scripts and many servers, the same steps run from a JSON file, without a browser:

bin/sutraflow install --config install.json [--dry-run]

Take the file the web installer saved on its Review page, or start from docs/install-example.json in the release, which shows every field. Passwords are never written in the file: give {"env": "NAME"} (an environment variable) or {"file": "path"} (a file holding only the password).

{
  "admin": { "username": "admin", "password": { "env": "SUTRA_INSTALL_ADMIN_PASSWORD" } },
  "database": { "kind": "postgres", "host": "db.internal", "database": "sutraflow", "user": "sutraflow",
                "password": { "env": "SUTRA_INSTALL_DB_PASSWORD" }, "sslMode": "verify", "create": true },
  "server": { "studioPort": 4800, "gatewayHttp": 8080, "gatewayHttps": 8443, "environment": "production" },
  "cluster": { "name": "Production" },
  "start": true
}
  • The whole file is checked first: every problem (a weak password, a busy port, a database that cannot be reached, pgvector missing) is reported at once, before anything changes.
  • --dry-run checks the file and prints the plan.
  • Exit code 0 when done, 1 when a step failed, 2 when the file is wrong. Progress goes to the terminal and to data/logs/installer.log.
  • Settings files for further cluster engines are written beside it as sutraflow-engine-<name>.env.

Silent upgrade

bin/sutraflow upgrade --config upgrade.json [--dry-run]
{ "from": "/opt/sutraflow", "backupDir": "/backups/sutraflow", "start": true }

Run it from the new release's folder; the steps are those of Upgrading, with the same exit codes.

5. Upgrading

Unpack the new release beside the installation (a folder of its own, never over it) and run bin/sutraflow upgrade from the new folder (Windows: bin\sutraflow.cmd upgrade). The installer opens on the Upgrade pages. It upgrades installations of 2.1.0 or later; an older one is upgraded by hand (below).

Example: a Laragon installation from 2.1.0 to 2.1.2

SutraFlow runs from C:\laragon\www\sutra (studio on 4810, data in C:\laragon\data\sutraflow, PostgreSQL). The new release goes into a folder of its own; the installation is never unzipped over.

  1. Unpack sutraflow-2.1.2-windows-x64-offline.zip anywhere else, for example C:\SutraFlow-2.1.2.
  2. From that folder run bin\sutraflow.cmd upgrade. The upgrade pages open in the browser.
  3. On Installation give C:\laragon\www\sutra and choose Check: it shows 2.1.0, its PostgreSQL database and data folder.
  4. On Review keep the backup folder empty (it becomes C:\laragon\www\sutra\backups\2.1.0-<time>) and Start it again ticked; choose Upgrade.
  5. When Done says 2.1.0 to 2.1.2, SutraFlow answers on 4810 again with the new version. C:\SutraFlow-2.1.2 can be deleted; 4810 keeps running from C:\laragon\www\sutra.

Apache, a terminal or Explorer open in C:\laragon\www\sutra can stay open. Unzipping over the installation yourself is the manual way below: it has no backup and no way back of its own.

Deployed Sutras and work in flight

  • Deployed Sutras stay deployed at their versions: they are in the database, which the upgrade keeps (and compares).
  • The stop is graceful: running steps finish first.
  • Waiting work (approvals, timers, queued runs, steps waiting to retry, runs waiting for a connection) is kept in the database and taken up by the new version when it starts.
  • During the upgrade the gateway does not answer: callers of REST, SOAP and MCP services get no reply for those minutes, and listeners pick up files and messages afterwards. Choose a quiet time. In a cluster, upgrade every engine's folder before starting any (below).

Engines and the cluster after installing

The upgrade keeps every engine and cluster setting as it is. They are changed at any time, without upgrading, in the Admin Console:

SettingAt installationLater
Cluster nameCluster pageEngines, Rename the cluster; sutra engines cluster-name "Shop cluster"
Engine names people readCluster pageEngines, Rename; sutra engines name <id> "Shop engine 2"
Engine id (SUTRA_ENGINE_ID)Cluster pageStays: the steps an engine ran record it. Only its display name changes
May leadCluster pageEngines, Never lead / May lead; sutra engines lead <engine> --yes|--no
Node memory of each engineServer and Cluster pagesEngines, Tuning, Node memory, then Restart
An engine beside the studioServer pageIts ports in sutraflow.env (ENGINE_PORT, ENGINE_GATEWAY_HTTP, ENGINE_GATEWAY_HTTPS), then sutraflow start engine
An engine on another machineCluster page writes its settings fileInstall the same version there with the same SUTRA_DB and a copy of data/master.key, then sutraflow start engine (Setting up a cluster)

Installation

Give the folder of the installation, for example C:\laragon\www\sutra or /opt/sutraflow, and choose Check: it shows the version, the database, the data folder and the address found there, and whether it can be upgraded to this version.

Ports need not be given. The upgrade reads them, with the data folder and the database, from the installation's own sutraflow.env, uses them to stop and start it and to check that it answers, and keeps them. This holds for SutraFlow started through its launcher (sutraflow start, the Laragon Procfile, the Windows task or systemd unit of sutraflow service). A process started by hand with other settings in its environment cannot be reached by the upgrade: stop it yourself first.

Review

The version from and to, and the backup folder: empty means backups inside the installation. Nothing changes until you choose Upgrade.

What the upgrade does

  1. Snapshot of the data: every table's row count and a checksum, read without changing anything.
  2. Stop: the studio and the engine beside it stop gracefully: no new work, running steps finish (since 2.1.2 the engine beside the studio stops too, so nothing runs on a program or database that is changing).
  3. Program files free: every program file must be replaceable. A file another program holds without sharing stops the upgrade here, before anything changes, with the file and, on Windows, the process that holds it (its id and name), so you can stop that program and run the upgrade again. A folder that is merely open, a web server such as Apache or IIS serving from it, a terminal or Explorer in it, does not stop it.
  4. Backup into backups/<old version>-<time>: the data folder with master.key, sutraflow.env, and for PostgreSQL a pg_dump that is read back with pg_restore --list before anything changes (a backup that cannot be read stops the upgrade here). Without pg_dump on the machine, SutraFlow copies the database itself.
  5. Move the old runtime aside into the backup, and install the new one. A folder another program is in cannot be moved on Windows: it is copied into the backup and its files are replaced in place instead, and the step says which. The data folder, sutraflow.env and a site's own .htaccess and web.config stay where they are.
  6. New settings are added to sutraflow.env with their defaults; your values are kept.
  7. Database changes of the new version, then Compare the data with the snapshot: every table must hold what it held.
  8. Start and Check: the studio, and the engine beside it if it was running, start again and must answer with the new version.

When a step fails

The previous version is put back: the old runtime, the data folder and sutraflow.env from the backup, the database from its dump, and the previous version started again. The page and data/logs/installer.log say which step failed and why. A database restore waits at most a minute for tables another process still holds (an engine on another machine of the cluster) and then reports that the database was not restored, with the backup to restore by hand, instead of waiting for ever (2.1.2).

Clusters

Stop the engines on the other machines first, upgrade every engine's folder, then start them. Engines of different versions must not run on one database: the newer version's database changes are made for its own program.

By hand, and from before 2.1.0

  1. Stop gracefully: sutraflow stop all.
  2. Back up the data folder (with master.key) and, for PostgreSQL, the database (pg_dump -Fc).
  3. Unpack the new release beside the old one; bring over sutraflow.env and the data folder (or keep SUTRA_DATA_DIR pointing at it).
  4. sutraflow setup (installs the runtime packages unless the release is offline), then sutraflow start. The database is upgraded at start.
Before an upgrade

Read the release notes' What changes for you.
Make sure the backup folder has room for the data folder and a dump of the database.
Keep the backup until the new version has run for a while: it is the way back.

6. Development machines: Laragon and Linux

Windows: Laragon

For development and proofs of concept on Windows, Laragon is a convenient base: one installer brings Apache, MySQL, PostgreSQL, PHP, Node.js and HeidiSQL, starts them from one window, and keeps everything under C:\laragon. The DB Ops samples use its MySQL as it comes (127.0.0.1:3306, user root, no password), and SutraFlow can keep its own data in its PostgreSQL.

  1. Install Laragon (the full edition) and click Start All.
  2. Unpack a release into C:\laragon\www\sutra and run bin\sutraflow.cmd install; or copy deploy/laragon/sutraflow.env beside it for the usual Laragon layout: studio on 4810 (gateway 8090), engine on 4811 (gateway 8091), data in C:\laragon\data\sutraflow outside the web folder.
  3. For http://sutra.test, copy deploy/laragon/01-sutra.conf to C:\laragon\etc\apache2\sites-enabled: it loads Apache's proxy modules and forwards the name to the studio.
  4. Let Laragon start it: Menu > Procfile, add SutraFlow: autorun C:\laragon\www\sutra\bin\sutraflow.cmd start --foreground PWD=www/sutra.
  5. Every other command is the launcher: bin\sutraflow.cmd status, stop all, start engine, cli sutras list, open admin.

HeidiSQL and PostgreSQL

HeidiSQL needs the PostgreSQL client library to open a PostgreSQL session; without it the connection fails with a missing libpq.dll. Choose the library in the session's Library field from C:\laragon\bin\postgresql\<version>\bin\libpq.dll, or copy libpq.dll with the libcrypto-*.dll and libssl-*.dll (and, when present, libiconv-*.dll and libintl-*.dll) from that folder into C:\laragon\bin\heidisql. pgAdmin and DBeaver bring their own drivers.

pgvector for Laragon's PostgreSQL

A knowledge base stored in PostgreSQL needs the pgvector extension, and the installer requires it unless you go on without it. Laragon's PostgreSQL does not include it; add a Windows build for the same major version:

  1. Find the version: in Laragon's terminal run postgres -V (for example 18).
  2. Download a Windows x64 build of pgvector for that version. pgvector itself publishes source only; community builds exist (for example the pgvector_pgsql_windows releases on GitHub). Use one you trust.
  3. Stop PostgreSQL in Laragon; copy lib\vector.dll into C:\laragon\bin\postgresql\<version>\lib\ and the files of share\extension\ into C:\laragon\bin\postgresql\<version>\share\extension\; start it again.
  4. Check: SELECT name, default_version FROM pg_available_extensions WHERE name = 'vector'; returns a row. The installer's Test connection then enables it.

Linux

PartDebian / UbuntuFedora / RHEL
Node.js 24Through nvm (nvm install 24), or the NodeSource packages.
MySQL or MariaDBsudo apt install mariadb-serversudo dnf install mariadb-server
PostgreSQLsudo apt install postgresql (newer versions from the PostgreSQL apt repository)sudo dnf install postgresql-server, then sudo postgresql-setup --initdb
pgvectorsudo apt install postgresql-<version>-pgvectorsudo dnf install pgvector_<version>

With Docker, docker run -d --name sutra-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev -p 5432:5432 pgvector/pgvector:pg17 gives PostgreSQL with pgvector, and docker run -d --name sutra-mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=dev -p 3306:3306 mysql:8.4 adds MySQL. Then install SutraFlow with bin/sutraflow install, and bin/sutraflow service prints a systemd unit to start it with the machine.

Development only

Laragon and these Linux set-ups are for development machines. For servers, run SutraFlow as a service or in Docker with a managed PostgreSQL (Running in production).

Running SutraFlow

7. The sutraflow command and server settings

Every way of running SutraFlow uses one launcher: bin/sutraflow on Linux and macOS, bin\sutraflow.cmd on Windows (sutraflow after npm install -g). Its settings are in sutraflow.env beside it, written by the installer (ports, SUTRA_DATA_DIR, SUTRA_DB, SUTRA_NODE and any other SUTRA_ setting); SUTRAFLOW_ENV points it at another settings file.

CommandDoes
install, upgradeThe web installer or the upgrade pages; with --config file.json silently (The web installer, Upgrading)
start, start engineThe studio, or a headless engine beside it on the same database, in the background; output in <data>/logs/<name>.out.log. --foreground keeps it in the terminal, for services and Laragon
stop, stop engine, stop allGraceful: no new work, running steps finish first; --force ends a process that does not stop within 45 s
restart, status, logs [--follow]Restart; ready or not, process, addresses and database; the output log
open [designer|admin|guide|admin-guide|architecture]Opens the page in the browser
cli ...The sutra command against this studio with the local admin token (data/admin-token.txt)
db info, db copy --to ...The database in use and its row counts; copy to PostgreSQL
serviceA systemd unit (Linux) or a scheduled task (Windows) to start with the machine
setup [--ports]The runtime packages (npm ci --omit=dev), the settings file and the local admin token, for installing by hand
docker up|down|status|logs|build, docker cluster ...docker-compose.yml (a studio and an engine) or docker-compose.cluster.yml (PostgreSQL, a studio and two engines); missing passwords and the master key are made once into .env

The full list, read from the launcher itself, is in the Command reference.

Server settings

Set in sutraflow.env (or the environment of a service or container). The installer writes the first ones; Admin Console, Engines, Tuning changes several of them while SutraFlow runs, and its values win until cleared.

VariableDefaultMeaning
SUTRA_MODEstudiostudio, or engine (headless)
SUTRA_ENVIRONMENTdevelopment (studio), production (engine)development, test or production: shown on every log line and audit entry; a production server takes Sutras only from releases
SUTRA_DATA_DIR./dataDatabase file, vault key, logs
SUTRA_DB, SUTRA_DB_PASSWORDSQLitepostgres://user@host:5432/db and its password, kept apart
SUTRA_MASTER_KEYthe key fileThe vault key, base64 32 bytes; the same on every engine
SUTRA_ADMIN_HOST, SUTRA_ADMIN_PORT127.0.0.1, 4800Studio and admin API (STUDIO_PORT, ENGINE_PORT in sutraflow.env)
SUTRA_GATEWAY_HTTP_PORT, SUTRA_GATEWAY_HTTPS_PORT8080, 8443Gateway, until changed in Admin Console, Server, Gateway & TLS
SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKEN(none)Bearer token for the command line and automation; acts as an administrator. Prefer system account tokens, limited by their roles
SUTRA_ENGINE_IDcomputer nameThis engine's name in a cluster (STUDIO_ENGINE_ID, ENGINE_ENGINE_ID)
SUTRA_CAN_LEAD10: this engine never leads (also May lead in Engines)
STUDIO_MEMORY_MB, ENGINE_MEMORY_MB0Node memory of each process; 0 lets Node.js decide
SUTRA_WORKERSby machineSteps run at once (4 on 1 vCPU / 1 GB up to 32 on 8 cores); 0 = serve only
SUTRA_MEMORY_WORKERS0Steps at once for Sutras that run in memory; 0 = as SUTRA_WORKERS
SUTRA_POLL_MSby machineHow often an idle engine looks for due steps (200 to 500 ms)
SUTRA_SETTINGS_REFRESH_MSby machineHow long an engine keeps Project and Engine properties; 0 = every step
SUTRA_PG_POOLhalf of SUTRA_WORKERS (4 to 20)Connections of an engine's PostgreSQL pool; keep engines × (pool + 1) under max_connections
SUTRA_PG_NOTIFY10: no LISTEN/NOTIFY wake hint (polling only)
SUTRA_DEPLOY_DIR(none)Folder of packages deployed at start
SUTRA_PUBLIC_URL(none)The studio address as people reach it behind a proxy (single sign-on)

SUTRA_LOG_FORMAT, SUTRA_METRICS_TOKENtext, (none)json: log lines on standard output; bearer token for /metrics
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_SERVICE_NAME(none), sutraflowOpenTelemetry collector (OTLP/HTTP) and the service name on traces
SUTRA_DNS_SERVERS(none)DNS servers for the Node process only (for example for MongoDB SRV records)

8. Where SutraFlow keeps its data

Everything SutraFlow knows is in one database and one data folder. This chapter says what is where, what is encrypted, what grows, and how to back it up. Look, but change things through the designer, the Admin Console or the sutra command: they check permissions, write the audit log and keep the engines in step, which a direct database change does not.

The database

  • SQLite (the start): the file <data>/sutra.db. Open it read-only with DB Browser for SQLite or HeidiSQL, ideally from a copy.
  • PostgreSQL (after Moving to PostgreSQL): the database named in SUTRA_DB, for example sutraflow, schema public. In HeidiSQL or pgAdmin, open that database; the server's other databases (such as postgres) hold nothing of SutraFlow.

Text columns hold JSON and ISO dates, so the same tables work on both databases and move between them as they are. The Admin Console's Database page shows which database is in use and its main row counts.

The data folder

In <data>What
master.keyThe key that encrypts the vault, OAuth and Git tokens and the TLS key (made with the first secret). Without it those values cannot be read: back it up apart from the database, and keep it secret. SUTRA_MASTER_KEY can give it instead.
sutra.dbThe SQLite database (kept as a backup after a move to PostgreSQL).
admin-token.txtThe local admin token the launcher uses to stop and query the server.
logs/Project logs and the server's output log.
files/<project>/Each project's files folder (${files} in variables): documents, scripts and files that release zips bring.
workspaces/Git working copies of projects in Git.
knowledge/Knowledge bases kept in a folder.
config/Deployment configs dropped here as <project>.json are loaded at start.
run/, migration/The launcher's process ids; the status and log of a move to PostgreSQL.

The tables

36 tables, by what they are for. Encrypted marks values only readable with the master key; Grows marks tables that get longer with use, and what keeps them in check.

Projects and Sutras

TableHoldsColumns
projectsProjects with their variables, logging and deployment config.id name description config updated_at owner restricted
flowsSutra drafts: the document being edited and its latest version number.id name doc version updated_at project_id folder
flow_versionsPublished, unchangeable versions of each Sutra. Grows: one row per published version; kept for rollback.flow_id version doc note created_at

resourcesConnections, security profiles, API policies, AI providers and MCP servers (secret names only).id kind name config updated_at folder project_id

foldersExplorer folders of a project kept while nothing is in them, per area (sutras, resources, schemas, wsdl); each item keeps its own folder in a folder column.project_id area path
countersCounter activity values per project.project_id name value updated_at
mem_rowsThe database copy of memory tables kept with a failsafe: key, row, expiry, and the version of the change that wrote it (a removed row keeps its key with no row).store_id k value expires_at version
mem_metaPer memory table: the latest change version and when it was last loaded from its source, so engines pick up each other's changes.store_id version loaded_at reload_at

Runs and the work queue

TableHoldsColumns
runsOne row per run: the Sutra document it started with, status, trigger input, state (outputs, variables, branch tokens, logs) and times. Grows: one row per run; housekeeping deletes runs older than the retention days (Admin Console > Engines > Tuning).id flow_id flow_name version doc status source trigger_node input state error steps started_at finished_at started_by project_id debug priority
tasksOne row per step execution: status, attempt, not-before time, owner engine and claim number (counted up at each claim, for fencing), input, output, port, wait details, error and duration. The work queue. Grows: one row per step; deleted with their run.id run_id node_id input status attempt not_before phase port output error ms wait started_at finished_at released owner priority queued_at claim
connection_permitsOne row per place in use on a limited connection (Maximum concurrent activities). kind task: a durable step, valid while its claim (task, owner, claim) is running. kind lease: a listener poll or background job, valid until expires_at and renewed while held. Ended claims and expired leases are removed at the next admission.resource_id task_id owner claim kind holder project since expires_at
connection_waitsSteps waiting for a limited connection: the connection, the reason shown in the Admin Console, since when, and how many times it was checked (the pause between checks grows to 5 s). Removed when the step runs or leaves the queue.task_id resource_id reason since checks
connection_usageSamples of each limited connection (in use, waiting, limit) taken by the leader every 30 s for the Admin Console graphs; kept 7 days.at resource_id active waiting limit_n
run_outputsThe output of each step of a run, one row per step name (a later pass of a loop replaces it), read by the steps after it. Kept apart from the run state so a step writes only its own output. Grows: one row per step name of a run; deleted with their run.run_id name out
payloadsLarge parts of a run's input (over 256 KB: a broker message body, a file's content), stored once (2.1.1); the run's data carries a reference to them and each step gets the whole value back. Grows: one row per large input part of a run; deleted with their run.id run_id size data created_at
approval_votesEach approver's decision on an approval: the step's task, the username, approved or not, the comment, when, and whether an administrator decided on behalf of the approvers.task_id username approved comment at on_behalf

Releases and the cluster

TableHoldsColumns
package_deploymentsPackage history per project: version, checksum, who deployed it, the report and the package itself (for rollback). Grows: one row per package deployment, with the package; kept for rollback.id seq project_id name version checksum deployed_at deployed_by report package
enginesEngines of the cluster: host, process, mode, version, heartbeat, workers, active steps, draining.id host pid mode version started_at heartbeat_at workers active draining drain_requested can_lead memory restart_requested

file_listener_stateOne row per deployed file trigger after its first folder baseline, shared by leaders so a takeover does not baseline the folder again.flow_id node_id

bus_messagesDurable queue/topic delivery identities and their reserved run: Kafka offset or RabbitMQ/AMQP message id, used to avoid starting a second run after redelivery or leader takeover. Grows: one row per protected broker delivery; failed deliveries are removed for retry and completed identities follow run retention.flow_id node_id message_key run_id status updated_at

Backups

  • SQLite: stop SutraFlow (or use sqlite3 sutra.db ".backup copy.db" while it runs) and copy the whole data folder.
  • PostgreSQL: pg_dump -Fc sutraflow > sutraflow.dump (or the hosted service's backups), plus the data folder without sutra.db.
  • Always master.key, kept apart from the database backup: a stolen database backup without the key reveals no secrets.
  • Restore: put the folder and the key back (and pg_restore for PostgreSQL), then start SutraFlow.

9. Moving to PostgreSQL

SutraFlow keeps its own data (projects, Sutras, runs, people, the vault) in SQLite until you move it to PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL lets several engines share the data and holds more. The move takes a minute and is one button in the Admin Console, or one script on Windows and Linux.

Do you need to move?

On a single server, SQLite needs no database server and handles about 420 small steps a second. Move when you add engines, need failover, need more throughput on one busy server, or must run the database apart. See Sizing and performance.

1. Prepare PostgreSQL

  • On this machine (Laragon includes PostgreSQL), on another server, or hosted: Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Amazon RDS, Google Cloud SQL. Version 14 or later.
  • A user for SutraFlow with a password. Either an empty database it owns (CREATE DATABASE sutraflow OWNER sutra;), or CREATEDB, so the move makes the database.
  • Remote servers: PostgreSQL must listen on the network (listen_addresses), its pg_hba.conf must accept the SutraFlow machine (for example hostssl sutraflow sutra 10.0.0.15/32 scram-sha-256), and the firewall or network security group must open port 5432 to it. Hosted services do this in their portal.
  • Knowledge bases stored in PostgreSQL also need pgvector; SutraFlow's own data does not.

2. Save and test the connection

Reconnecting after a lost connection

On PostgreSQL, the Database page also sets how an engine opens its database connection again after it was lost (a database restart, a network cut): Tries (1 to 5, default 1), Wait between tries (0 to 2,000 ms, default 500) and Time per try (0.5 to 10 s, default 3). The engine pauses while a statement waits for the connection, so the page shows the longest pause these give; keep it to a few seconds. A statement that cannot reach the database fails at once and the work around it retries on its own: steps by their retry settings, listeners at their next poll, the cluster heartbeat at its next beat. Start-up always tries 10 times with growing waits. The settings apply to the engine you save them on at once and to the others at their next start. (Before 2.1.0 a lost connection was tried 10 times with growing waits, which held an engine still for about 40 seconds.)

Admin Console → Server → Database shows the database in use. Fill in host, port, database, user, password and SSL:

SSLUse for
offPostgreSQL on this machine or a trusted private network
requireEncrypted; the server's certificate is not checked. Servers with their own (self-signed) certificate
verifyEncrypted and the certificate checked against the host name. Hosted PostgreSQL (Azure, AWS, Google Cloud)

Test connection signs in and reports the PostgreSQL version, whether it signed in with the password and over SSL, whether the database exists or will be made, pgvector, and SutraFlow tables already there. Its messages say what to fix: a refused password, a host name that cannot be found, a port a firewall blocks, a server that does not accept this machine (pg_hba.conf) or wants SSL, a certificate that cannot be checked. Save keeps the connection; the password goes to the vault and never comes back to the page. A changed connection must be tested again before it can be used.

3. Migrate

Migrate now runs tools/migrate-to-postgres. The page shows each step and waits while SutraFlow restarts:

  1. SutraFlow stops gracefully: no new work, running steps finish. Triggers and APIs pause for about a minute.
  2. Every table is copied to PostgreSQL (the database is made when missing), and the rows of every table are counted on both sides.
  3. sutraflow.env gets SUTRA_DB=postgres://user@host:5432/sutraflow and the password apart as SUTRA_DB_PASSWORD (so the address can be shown and logged); the old file is kept beside it; on Linux the file is made readable only by its owner.
  4. SutraFlow starts again (and the engine, when it was running) and must answer on PostgreSQL.
  5. If the copy or the start fails, the old sutraflow.env is put back and SutraFlow starts on SQLite again. The SQLite file is never changed, so it stays as a backup.

Tick Replace SutraFlow tables already in the target database only to overwrite an earlier copy.

By hand, or on a server without the Admin Console

tools\migrate-to-postgres.cmd                         (Windows)
tools/migrate-to-postgres.sh                          (Linux, macOS)
tools/migrate-to-postgres.sh --url "postgres://sutra:password@db.example.com:5432/sutraflow?sslmode=verify-full"

Without --url the script uses the connection saved on the Database page. It needs SutraFlow started with the launcher (sutraflow start, the Laragon Procfile, the Windows task or the systemd unit), because it stops and starts it. With a systemd unit, stop the service first, run the script, then start the service again. Progress goes to the console and to <data>/migration/status.json; the full output is in <data>/migration/migration.log.

Afterwards

  • Back up PostgreSQL (pg_dump, or the hosted service's backups); the master key in the data folder still decrypts the vault and must be kept with the backups.
  • More engines on other machines use the same SUTRA_DB, SUTRA_DB_PASSWORD and master key (see Running in production).
  • To go back to SQLite: stop SutraFlow, put the kept sutraflow.env.sqlite-... file back, start it (changes made on PostgreSQL stay there).

10. Monitoring, runs and housekeeping

EndpointPurpose
GET /healthLiveness: the process answers
GET /readyReadiness: storage answers, packages are deployed, the gateway listens, not draining; 503 with reasons otherwise. The health check for load balancers
GET /metricsPrometheus text, per engine; protect it with SUTRA_METRICS_TOKEN

Metrics

  • sutra_runs_started_total{sutra,source}, sutra_runs_finished_total{sutra,status}, sutra_run_duration_seconds
  • sutra_steps_total{activity,outcome} (done, error handled by an error output, failed), sutra_step_duration_seconds, sutra_step_retries_total
  • sutra_gateway_requests_total{kind,status}, sutra_gateway_request_duration_seconds
  • sutra_tasks{status}, sutra_engine_running_steps, sutra_engine_workers, sutra_engine_leader, sutra_engines_alive, sutra_listeners{state}, sutra_info{version,mode,engine}
  • PostgreSQL pool: sutra_db_pool_connections, sutra_db_pool_waiting, sutra_db_pool_acquire_ms, sutra_db_transaction_ms; sutra_event_loop_delay_ms

Traces and logs

  • Set OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT (an OpenTelemetry collector, Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb): a run is one trace with a span per step (activity, outcome, attempt, engine, error), across engines; a caller's traceparent is continued and every gateway answer carries the run's.
  • SUTRA_LOG_FORMAT=json writes one JSON object per line on standard output: time, level, engine, project, Sutra, run, step, message. Each project's own log file stays as configured.
  • The launcher's output log of each process: <data>/logs/studio.out.log, engine.out.log; the installer's: installer.log.

Runs and housekeeping

  • Finished runs (done, failed, cancelled) older than SUTRA_RUN_RETENTION_DAYS (30; 0 keeps everything, per Sutra in its tuning) are deleted with their steps by the leader, about once a minute. Waiting runs, such as approvals and timers, are never deleted. Admin Console, Engines, Delete old runs now runs it at once.
  • Run again from the failed step (Admin Console, Traceability or Applications, Runs; sutra runs resubmit <id>): the failed step runs again with the same input; everything the earlier steps produced is kept.
  • Audit entries older than SUTRA_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS (365) are deleted the same way; Admin Console, Audit log has the retention and clearing.

Alerts that tell people when something goes wrong (failed runs, slow runs, gateway errors, engines down, work waiting, certificates ending) are set in the Admin Console: Alerts.

Engines and clusters

11. Running in production: engines, Docker, clusters

Headless engines

The same program started with SUTRA_MODE=engine runs Sutras without the studio: no designer pages and no editing. It keeps /health, /ready and /metrics, the Admin Console at /admin for its users, and an automation API for API tokens (the admin token or system account tokens). Packages in SUTRA_DEPLOY_DIR are deployed when it starts; a package that cannot be deployed stops the start.

Docker

docker build -t sutraflow:2.1.0 .
docker run -e SUTRA_MODE=engine -e SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKEN=... -e SUTRA_MASTER_KEY=... \
           -v ./deploy:/deploy:ro -p 8080:8080 sutraflow:2.1.0

The image runs as a non-root user, checks its own health, and writes JSON logs. docker-compose.yml has a studio and an engine; docker-compose.cluster.yml has PostgreSQL, a studio and two engines.

Clusters

Several engines share one database (SUTRA_DB=postgres://...), each with its own SUTRA_ENGINE_ID and all with the same SUTRA_MASTER_KEY.

A cluster needs a load balancer

  • Put a load balancer in front of the engines' gateways (Apache, nginx, IIS, a cloud load balancer) and send every caller of REST, SOAP, MCP and agent services to it, with /ready on the admin port as the health check. A run starts on the engine that receives its call. Measured: four engines did about three times the work of one with calls spread over them, and little more than one when every call went to the same engine.
  • Timers, folder and mailbox listeners run on the leader only, so they never start twice; the steps that follow are shared by every engine.
  • Sutras that run in memory stay on the engine that started them: only a load balancer spreads them.

Database connections

Remote activity databases. Resources → Database connection accepts the remote host and service port for PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQL Server and Oracle. These activity connections are separate from the engine's own SUTRA_DB. Configure network/firewall access, a least-privilege database user and a vault password. For PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQL Server, enable TLS; use the server certificate's DNS host and paste a private CA PEM into Trusted database CA when needed. Certificate verification remains enabled by default. Project/Engine properties can supply environment-specific fields. Oracle can use a DBA-supplied connect string (including supported TCPS/wallet configuration); consult its driver documentation. SQLite is a local file, not a remote database service: do not use a shared network SQLite file for a cluster.

On 24 October 2026, external PostgreSQL 17.2 and MariaDB 11.8.9 endpoints passed bound queries and rollback through the PostgreSQL and MySQL connectors with client TLS verification enabled. The PostgreSQL endpoint negotiated client TLS 1.3, but its pool-to-database backend reported no TLS; check the provider's internal transport policy. The MariaDB endpoint used port 3306 and TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384. These short connector checks are not the separate-machine 24-hour engine soak or SQL Server/Oracle certification.

  • On PostgreSQL each engine runs its steps through a pool of connections (SUTRA_PG_POOL, by default half of Steps at once, from 4 to 20) and keeps one more for everything else. Many steps then have their database work in flight at once.
  • Keep engines × (pool + 1), plus the studio and your own tools, under PostgreSQL's max_connections (100 by default). Four engines with a pool of 8 use 36.
  • /metrics shows the pool: sutra_db_pool_connections, sutra_db_pool_waiting (transactions waiting for a connection), sutra_db_pool_acquire_ms and sutra_db_transaction_ms. Waiting that grows means the pool is too small for the work; transactions that grow mean the database is the limit.
  • SUTRA_PG_ASYNC=0 runs the engine through one synchronous connection as before 1.7.6: a fallback, several times slower.
  • PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY wakes engines when committed work enters the durable queue. Polling remains active as the correctness fallback. Set SUTRA_PG_NOTIFY=0 only to disable the wake hint.

Engine names. SUTRA_ENGINE_ID is an engine's identity in the cluster: the steps it runs record it as their owner, and the leader uses it to hand a stopped engine's steps to the others. Without it, the launcher uses the computer name (vm-west-01-studio, vm-west-01-engine); the Laragon set-up names its engines laragon and laragon-engine. Set it once per engine (in sutraflow.env: STUDIO_ENGINE_ID, ENGINE_ENGINE_ID) and keep it. For the name people see, use Rename in Admin Console → Engines or sutra engines name <id> "Azure West Europe 1": a display name that can change at any time.

  • Work is shared, and each step is run by exactly one engine.
  • One engine leads and runs timers and folder, mailbox, queue and Drive listeners, so they fire once. If it stops, another takes over within a few heartbeats.
  • Steps of an engine that stopped are finished by another.
  • Callers get their replies from whichever engine they reached.
  • A deploy reaches every engine.

Step-by-step set-ups for one machine, two machines, engines only and Docker are in Setting up a cluster, step by step. SUTRA_CAN_LEAD=0 keeps an engine from ever leading.

Engines with SUTRA_WORKERS=0 only serve APIs. sutra status or GET /api/engine/status lists the engines, the leader and the queue.

Stopping without losing work

On docker stop, Ctrl+C or POST /api/engine/drain, an engine:

  1. reports not ready, so load balancers stop sending it requests;
  2. hands leadership over;
  3. lets running steps finish for SUTRA_DRAIN_MS, and hands the rest back to the queue for another engine;
  4. closes.

Monitoring

WhatWhere
Liveness and readiness/health, /ready on the admin port
Metrics/metrics (Prometheus): runs, steps by outcome, retries, durations, gateway requests, queue, leader, listeners
TracesSet OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: each run is a trace with a span per step, continuing a caller's traceparent
LogsSUTRA_LOG_FORMAT=json: one JSON line per event on standard output, plus each project's log file

Runs

Finished runs older than SUTRA_RUN_RETENTION_DAYS (30 by default) are deleted; waiting runs are kept. A failed run can continue with Run again from the failed step in Runs: the failed step runs again with the same input, and the earlier steps' results are kept.

Checklist

  1. Set SUTRA_MASTER_KEY from your secret store, the same on every engine.
  2. Keep the studio on 127.0.0.1 or behind a VPN. Expose only the engines' gateway ports, behind a load balancer pointed at /ready.
  3. Set a long SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKEN; give it only to the release pipeline.
  4. Set the gateway certificate and require HTTPS in every API policy.
  5. Put environment-specific values in the deployment config, with ${env:NAME} for anything secret or host-specific.
  6. Release with packages; keep the files, they are your rollback.
  7. Back up the database (or the data folder).

Settings for every engine are in The sutraflow command and server settings; releases reach the engines as in Receiving releases on a server.

12. Setting up a cluster, step by step

A cluster is several SutraFlow processes (a studio and engines) sharing one PostgreSQL database. They share the work, and keep running when one of them stops. This chapter sets one up from scratch, for each common layout.

What every engine does, and what the leader does

Every process of a cluster is an engine: it runs steps, and it serves the gateway (REST, SOAP, WebSocket, MCP and agent services) on its own ports, applying the services' API security policies itself. There is no central gateway: a caller reaches whichever engine the load balancer picks, and that engine checks the caller, starts the run and answers.

One engine at a time is also the leader. The leader runs what must happen once in the cluster, not once per engine:

Every engineThe leader as well
Runs steps from the shared work queue (each step exactly once)Timers (each timer fires once, not once per engine)
Serves the gateway: REST, SOAP, WebSocket, MCP, chat, OpenAI-compatible and A2AListeners: folders, SFTP and FTP, mailboxes, queues and topics, Drive, Microsoft files, Discord, Telegram, Twitch, Data Factory, WebSocket client streams
Applies API security policies, validation and threat protection to its callersRecovery: steps of an engine that stopped are put back in the queue for the others
Writes a heartbeat every 5 secondsRun time limits, queued runs, alerts (every 30 seconds) and housekeeping (old runs, logs, audit)
Reloads deploys and settings on its next heartbeatForgetting engines that have been silent for ten minutes

The leader holds a lease in the database and renews it every heartbeat. If it stops renewing (stopped, crashed, cut off), the lease runs out after three heartbeats (15 seconds) and another engine takes it, starting the timers and listeners there. Nothing needs to be told: there is no leader to configure, only engines that may or may not lead (below).

Leader and gateway are separate

Security does not depend on the leader: each engine checks its own callers with the same policies, read from the shared database. A cluster whose leader stops keeps serving APIs on every other engine without a pause; only timers and listeners wait up to 15 seconds for the new leader.

The settings that make a cluster

SettingOn every process
SUTRA_DBThe same PostgreSQL address (postgres://user@host:5432/sutraflow), with SUTRA_DB_PASSWORD when it needs a password.
SUTRA_MASTER_KEYThe same key on every machine (it decrypts the vault). Copy it from the first machine's data/master.key, or put it in each sutraflow.env.
SUTRA_ENGINE_IDDifferent on every process: its name in the cluster. The launcher names them <computer>-studio and <computer>-engine (STUDIO_ENGINE_ID, ENGINE_ENGINE_ID in sutraflow.env to choose).
SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKENOptional; the same long token lets one release pipeline talk to every engine.
SUTRA_CAN_LEAD0 on engines that must never lead, for example machines that cannot reach the folders the folder triggers watch. At least one process must be able to lead.
SUTRA_PG_POOLOptional: connections per engine. Keep processes × (pool + 1) under PostgreSQL's max_connections.
SUTRA_PG_NOTIFYPostgreSQL queue wake hint (default on). Set to 0 to use polling alone; polling always remains enabled.

Before you start: PostgreSQL

  1. Install PostgreSQL 14 or later on its own machine (or use a managed service). On one test machine, the local one will do.
  2. Create a database and a user: CREATE USER sutra_owner PASSWORD '...'; CREATE DATABASE sutraflow OWNER sutra_owner;
  3. Allow the engine machines in pg_hba.conf (with scram-sha-256), and turn SSL on for anything that crosses a network.
  4. If you already have data in SQLite, move it once: Admin Console → Server → Database, or sutraflow db copy --to postgres://... (see Moving to PostgreSQL).

Layout 1: one machine, a studio and an engine

The simplest cluster, and a good way to try one: two processes on one server share the work, and one keeps serving while the other restarts.

  1. Install SutraFlow with PostgreSQL and A headless engine beside it (The web installer), or set SUTRA_DB in sutraflow.env of an existing installation to the PostgreSQL address.
  2. Start the studio: sutraflow start. It listens on 4800, its gateway on 8080 and 8443.
  3. Start an engine beside it: sutraflow start engine. It uses the same folder and settings, and listens on 4801, its gateway on 9080 and 9443 (ENGINE_PORT, ENGINE_GATEWAY_HTTP, ENGINE_GATEWAY_HTTPS).
  4. Check: sutraflow status, or Admin Console → Engines: two engines alive, one marked leader.
  5. Point your load balancer (or Apache or nginx on the same machine) at both gateways: 8080 and 9080, health check /ready on 4800 and 4801.
  6. Start both with the machine: sutraflow service prints the systemd units or the Windows scheduled tasks, one for the studio and one for the engine.

Layout 2: two machines, the studio and an engine on one, an engine on the other

  1. On machine A, set up layout 1, or just the studio.
  2. Copy data/master.key from machine A (or set SUTRA_MASTER_KEY on both).
  3. On machine B, install SutraFlow, and in its sutraflow.env set the same SUTRA_DB and SUTRA_MASTER_KEY, and SUTRA_ADMIN_HOST=0.0.0.0 only if a load balancer checks its /ready from another machine.
  4. Start only an engine on B: sutraflow start engine. Machine B has no studio: design on A, deploy from A, and B picks the deploy up on its next heartbeat.
  5. Check Admin Console → Engines on A: the engines of both machines are listed.
  6. Add B's gateway (9080, 9443) to the load balancer.
  7. Folder triggers: the leader may be either machine. Make the watched folders reachable from both (a shared drive), or set SUTRA_CAN_LEAD=0 on B so A always leads (and A's engines take over from each other).

Layout 3: engines only, behind a load balancer, with a separate studio

For production: no designer on the servers that serve traffic.

  1. Keep the studio on a design or test server; build releases there (Releases) or from Git in a pipeline (CI/CD).
  2. On each production machine install SutraFlow with the same SUTRA_DB (the production database) and SUTRA_MASTER_KEY, SUTRA_ENVIRONMENT=production, and start engines only: sutraflow start engine. On a machine with many cores, a second process (another folder with other ports) uses them better than one big one.
  3. Create the first administrator for the engines' Admin Console: sutraflow cli user add admin --role administrator.
  4. Deploy a release: sutra deploy release.zip against any engine (with its admin token), or drop the package in SUTRA_DEPLOY_DIR; every engine loads it.
  5. Put the load balancer in front of every engine's gateway port, health check /ready. Leave the admin ports (4801) on the private network.

Layout 4: Docker

sutraflow docker cluster up starts docker-compose.cluster.yml: PostgreSQL, a studio and two engines with the shared settings filled in. To add engines, copy the engine-2 service as engine-3 and so on, each with its own SUTRA_ENGINE_ID.

Which layout

NeedLayout
One server, more throughput, restarts without downtime1: studio and engine on one machine
Survive the loss of a machine2 or 3, with PostgreSQL replicated or managed
Separate design from production3: engines only in production
Containers or Kubernetes4: Docker, one engine per container

Checking a cluster

  • Admin Console → Engines: every engine, alive or not, the leader, steps running, never leads where set; drain one from there.
  • sutraflow status or GET /api/engine/status: the same as JSON.
  • /metrics: sutra_engine_leader is 1 on exactly one engine; sutra_engines_alive counts the others.
  • To restart an engine without losing work: sutraflow stop engine drains it (running steps finish or go back to the queue), then start it again.
Try a failover

With two engines running, stop the leader (sutraflow stop). Within 15 seconds the other one shows as leader in Engines, and its timers fire. Calls to the remaining gateway never stopped.

13. Sizing and performance

How much work a server takes, what to run on which machine, and the settings that change it. Every number here was measured with the load test that comes with SutraFlow (tools/loadtest.mjs), on the machine named under each table; run it on your own servers before you size production.

What a step costs

A Sutra runs durable by default: before a step starts, it is a row in the work queue, and when it ends, its output, the run state and the next steps are written in one database transaction. That is why a run survives a crash, a restart or a redeploy, and why it can wait for days for an approval. The price is a few database round trips per step. For most integrations this does not matter: a step that calls an API or a database takes 20 to 500 ms, and the engine's own work is 2 to 5 ms of it.

It matters when a Sutra has many tiny steps and must answer fast, such as a REST service that maps a request, checks it and replies in 30 ms. For those, a Sutra can run in memory.

Durable or in memory

Durable (default)In memory
Where the steps live while the run is openThe databaseA private in-memory database of the engine
Written to the databaseEvery stepOnce, when the run ends: the run and all its steps
A restart or crash while the run is openThe run carries on, on this engine or anotherThe run is lost (the caller gets an error or no answer)
Waits: approvals, Ask a person, Call Sutra with waitYesNo: the tuning is refused, or the step fails with the reason
Wait steps, timers, retries with a delayYesYes, within the engine
Run history, logs, resubmitYesYes, once the run has ended
Seen in Runs while open, cancelYesCancel yes; the run shows up in Runs when it ends
Small steps per second, one engine (measured below)about 120 on PostgreSQL, 520 on SQLiteabout 460 on PostgreSQL, 680 on SQLite
Which engine runs itAny engine of the cluster takes the next stepThe engine that started it runs all its steps: spread the callers over the engines (a load balancer in front of the gateways)

Set it per deployed Sutra: Admin Console > Applications > the Sutra > Tuning > Execution, or sutra sutras tune "Quote API" --project Shop --execution in-memory. Tests and debugging in the designer always run durable.

Choosing

In memory suits short request-reply Sutras (REST, SOAP and MCP services, lookups, mappings, validations) where a lost run is simply retried by the caller. Keep durable everything that moves money or data one way (orders, payments, file transfers, queue consumers that acknowledge), everything that waits, and every long run.

Machine profiles

When the environment does not set them, an engine takes its Steps at once, Queue check and Settings refresh from the profile of the machine it runs on: the smaller of what its cores and its memory allow. The engine reads its machine each time it starts, so the advice is for each install: a laptop, an Azure or Google VM of 2 vCPU, a container held to 1 core (a container limit counts). In a cluster, each engine reads its own machine.

Steps at once counts steps, not Sutras or palettes: a step is one activity box running in one run. With 32, an engine runs up to 32 boxes at the same moment, from any runs of any Sutras; the rest wait in the queue for a moment. Admin Console > Engines > Tuning > This machine shows the profile of the server, with Apply recommended tuning; sutra engines machine prints it.

ProfileMachineSteps at onceQueue checkEngines (PostgreSQL)Node memory per engineRead files whole up toRows per streamed batchDatabase
Small1 vCPU, 1 GB4500 ms1384 MB10 MB500SQLite
Small plus2 vCPU, 2 to 4 GB8250 ms11024 MB25 MB1000SQLite; PostgreSQL on another machine for a cluster
Medium4 vCPU, 8 GB16250 ms22048 MB50 MB2000SQLite for one engine at moderate load; PostgreSQL for a busy server or several engines
Large8 vCPU, 16 GB32200 ms43072 MB100 MB5000PostgreSQL for a busy server or several engines; SQLite for a moderate load
Very large16 vCPU or more, 32 GB or more32200 ms84096 MB200 MB5000PostgreSQL on its own machine, for several engines
  • Steps at once is more than the cores because most steps wait for a network or a database, and an engine runs other steps meanwhile. It does not speed up steps that only compute: in the measurements below, 32 steps at once did no better than 16. Raise it for Sutras that mostly wait (APIs, AI); lower it when steps compute (big mappings, scripts) and the engine CPU is near 1 core.
  • One engine is one Node.js process and uses about one core for its own work. To use more cores, run more engines on the same machine against PostgreSQL (the launcher starts them: sutraflow start engine), not more steps at once.
  • Node memory is the heap limit to give each engine (384 MB on the smallest machines, so the operating system and the database keep the rest). Each engine is its own Node.js process with its own memory: two engines on one machine each take their own share, they do not draw from one pool. Since 2.1.1 set it in the Admin Console under Engines, Tuning, Node memory (for every engine or one), with sutra engines tune --memory-mb, as STUDIO_MEMORY_MB or ENGINE_MEMORY_MB in sutraflow.env, or in the installer. It applies when the engine restarts: the engine writes the value to its own settings file and the Engines list shows restart for … MB with a Restart button, which lets running steps finish and starts it again. Engines started by a service manager or Docker do not restart themselves: use Drain and stop and set NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=… where they are started. The Engines list shows each engine's memory in use of its limit and the machine's memory.
  • SQLite runs inside the engine, with nothing to install: about 420 small steps a second on one engine. Use it on small machines (a PostgreSQL server needs its own few hundred MB) and for most single servers. PostgreSQL runs many steps' database work at the same time through a pool: about 720 small steps a second on one engine on the same machine, and 1,600 with four. Use it for several engines or machines, for failover, for a busy single server, or when the database must be managed apart, ideally on a machine (or a managed service) of its own.

SQLite or PostgreSQL

For smaller workloads, use SQLite. It is the default, needs nothing installed and nothing to look after: the database runs inside the engine. Measured with REST calls on one engine, SQLite ran about 420 small steps a second; held to one core and 512 MB, 365 a second durable and 750 in memory. PostgreSQL on the same machine ran about 720 on one engine (since 1.7.6 the engine works with PostgreSQL through a pool of connections) and 1,600 with four engines, so a busy server with a PostgreSQL server to hand gains from it.

Use SQLite whenUse PostgreSQL when
One server runs SutraFlow (a VM, a desktop, a Raspberry Pi class box)Several engines share the work, on one machine or several
Small and medium workloads: up to millions of steps a dayYou need failover: another engine takes over when one stops
Request-reply APIs and short Sutras at moderate volumeRuns must survive the loss of the whole machine (PostgreSQL replicated or managed)
Steady load up to a few hundred steps a secondA busy server that needs more (PostgreSQL ran about 70% more on one engine, four times as much with four)
Small machines (1 to 2 GB): no database server to feedYour company requires databases to be run, backed up and monitored by its DBAs
Development, testing, demos, edge sites, departmentsRun history must be queried by other tools while SutraFlow runs

Getting the most out of SQLite:

  • Keep the data folder on a local disk, ideally an SSD. Never on a network share (SMB, NFS): SQLite's locking is not safe there, and every write waits for the network.
  • Run one engine per data folder; for more throughput on the same machine, use Sutras that run in memory and raise Steps at once before you think of more engines. (Several engines on one SQLite file work, but they take turns to write, so they add little.)
  • Keep the database small: Keep finished runs at 7 to 30 days, and Step data in history on errors only or none for busy Sutras. A small database stays fast and backs up in seconds.
  • Back up while it runs with sqlite3 sutra.db ".backup copy.db", or stop SutraFlow and copy the data folder, together with master.key kept apart.
  • When you outgrow it (several engines, failover), the move to PostgreSQL is one button: see Moving to PostgreSQL. Nothing in the Sutras changes.
Rule of thumb

One server with a moderate load: SQLite, with the least to look after. A busy server, more than one engine, or a need for failover: PostgreSQL, ideally on a machine of its own.

What to run on which machine

MachineGood forAvoid
1 vCPU, 1 GB
(a small cloud VM, a Raspberry Pi class box)		Timers and file moves, a few REST or SOAP services, webhooks, email and chat notifications, SFTP transfers, CSV files of any size streamed in batches. Measured on one core with 512 MB and SQLite: 365 small durable steps a second (1.3 million an hour), 750 in memory. Real steps that call APIs take longer, so plan for tens of thousands of runs a day.Local AI models, Python steps that load big libraries, files read whole over 10 MB, a database server on the same machine, many Sutras with Runs at once above 20.
2 vCPU, 2 to 4 GBA department's integrations: tens of Sutras, REST APIs with in-memory Sutras for the fast ones, AI agents that call a cloud model, RAG over a folder with the built-in store, files read whole up to 25 MB.Local models above 3B parameters, PostgreSQL on the same machine with heavy runs.
4 vCPU, 8 GBProduction for a company: two engines and PostgreSQL, hundreds of Sutras, queue consumers (Kafka, RabbitMQ), databases, Databricks and Data Factory orchestration, small local models (Ollama phi4-mini class) for light use.Many local-model calls at once.
8 vCPU, 16 GBHeavy traffic: four engines, high-volume APIs, large file and data movements, local models of 7 to 8B parameters, vector stores (pgvector).Running the model, the database and the engines all on one machine at peak load.
16 vCPU and moreA cluster member, or several engines plus a gateway; PostgreSQL on its own machine.A single engine: it would use only a fraction of the machine.

Files: what size to read whole

  • A file read whole is held in memory several times over (bytes, text, rows, the step output), about 5 to 8 times its size for CSV. Keep Maximum size of Read file at or below the profile's Read files whole up to.
  • Bigger CSV and line files: tick Stream in batches (see Files). Memory then depends on the batch, not the file: a batch of 1,000 rows of 200 bytes is about 1 MB as data.
  • JSON and XML are read whole. For very big ones, ask the source for paged or line-delimited output (one JSON document per line, read as lines and streamed).
  • Binary files (base64) grow by a third in memory as text; move big binary files with Move / copy / delete file or SFTP, which stream, rather than reading them.
  • Each step output is kept in the run history up to 1 MB (bigger ones are cut to a preview). For Sutras that handle big data, set Step data in history to errors only or none.

Settings that change throughput

SettingWhereEffect
Steps at onceEngine tuning; SUTRA_WORKERSSteps one engine runs together. Too low: steps wait in the queue (see Queue wait in the Overview). Too high: memory and the database get busy.
Steps at once in memoryEngine tuning; SUTRA_MEMORY_WORKERSThe same for Sutras that run in memory; 0 = as Steps at once.
Queue checkEngine tuning; SUTRA_POLL_MSHow often an idle engine looks for due steps. Steps queued on the same engine start at once anyway; this only delays steps queued by another engine and retries. Lower answers sooner, higher saves database reads on small machines.
Settings refreshEngine tuning; SUTRA_SETTINGS_REFRESH_MSHow long an engine keeps Project and Engine properties before reading them again (a local administrator change applies at once, and the cluster signal clears other engines).
ExecutionSutra tuningDurable or in memory (above).
Runs at once, PrioritySutra tuningProtect a slow back end; let urgent Sutras go first.
Step data in historySutra tuningnone or errors only keeps the database small for busy Sutras.
Keep finished runsEngine and Sutra tuningFewer days, smaller database, faster history.

Measurements

The load test starts a studio and engines on a database of their own and runs a benchmark Sutra: a trigger and ten Transform steps, each computing a little and putting out the size of data shown. It counts finished steps per second, the time steps waited in the queue and took, what the database did, and the CPU and memory of the engines. Engines and PostgreSQL ran on the same machine, so the database took cores from the engines: a real cluster with PostgreSQL on its own server does better with several engines.
