An engine killed under load

Two engines, 600 REST calls spread over both gateways; the second engine was killed (no drain) when a third of the runs were done. Result: every run done, 0 failed, in 48.2 s (steps finished per engine: load-0 5527, load-1 1161). 24 calls that were in flight to the killed engine failed for their caller and were sent again to the other one, as a load balancer or a client retry does. The leader saw the dead engine after three missed heartbeats (15 s), put its running steps back in the queue, and the first engine finished them, also the runs of the calls that had failed. So a caller that retries can start a second run: make such Sutras safe to repeat (an idempotency key from the caller), as with any at-least-once system.

30 minutes of mixed work

Two engines for 30 minutes: a timer every 5 seconds, a Sutra that waits 2 seconds, one that always fails after two retries, the 5-step benchmark Sutra, and a redeploy halfway. 17,619 runs were started; Load 5x1KB: done 5873; Soak flaky: failed 5873; Soak timer: done 360; Soak wait: done 5873. Runs still open at the end: 0. The timer ran exactly once per 5 seconds in the whole cluster (from the leader only).

Memory of the busier engine, every minute of a 15-minute soak (MB): 173, 166, 190, 240, 241, 242, 242, 243, 244, 245, 246, 246, 244, 245, 245. It grows while caches and the heap warm up in the first minutes, then stays level: no leak.

A big file streamed on a small heap

One engine with Node held to 384 MB read a 1000 MB CSV file with Stream in batches (5000 rows per batch, a step per batch): done in 153 s (6.5 MB/s), 3729 steps, peak memory of the process 270 MB (144 MB at the start), database 4 MB at the end with Step data in history: none.

  • What changed in this release. Engines used to take one lock for every write in the cluster, so a second engine added nothing (82 steps a second with one engine or two); each run now has its own lock, and engines claim steps with skip locked. Project and Engine properties are cached for the settings refresh time instead of read for every step; the run state, step count and status are saved in one statement. Database transactions per step went from 14 to 7, and one engine went from 82 to about 120 steps a second. In memory, a step costs less than one transaction.
  • More engines scale when callers reach all of them, as behind a load balancer: with REST calls spread over the gateways, four engines did about three times the durable steps of one (352 against 116 a second), and in memory 1,660 against 540. When every run starts on one engine (a single timer, say), the others only help with the following steps, and in-memory runs not at all.
  • Bigger outputs cost more: each step writes its own output and reads the earlier ones. Since 1.8.0 (outputs kept apart from the run state) one engine on PostgreSQL ran 145 steps a second with 64 KB outputs (60 before), 40.7 with 256 KB (14.3) and 7.7 with 1 MB (2.6). For steps that pass large data along, keep the data in a file or a table and pass its name, or stream it.
  • No run failed and none was lost in any scenario, including the one where an engine was killed.

Measuring on your own servers

The soak, load and big-file test tools that produced these figures are in the source repository (they are not part of the release packages); how to run them is in SutraFlow Contributor Information. The full reports are in docs/benchmarks.

The Admin Console

14. The Admin Console

The Admin Console manages what is deployed: running projects and Sutras, approvals, engines, people, system accounts, roles and the audit log. Designing stays in the designer. Open it with Admin Console in the designer's top bar, or at /admin on the admin port (http://127.0.0.1:4800/admin). Headless engines serve the console too, without the designer.

Operate

  • Overview: tiles for engines, deployed Sutras, runs of the last 24 hours, waiting approvals, the work queue and the gateway certificate, and the latest failed runs with Resubmit. Test runs from the designer are not counted.
  • Applications: every deployed project with its package version and its Sutras: version, started or stopped, what starts it (REST path, SOAP path, timer, skill), runs of the last day and the last run. Stop makes the Sutra's triggers start nothing (its address answers 404, timers and listeners pause) while it stays deployed; Start brings it back on every engine; Restart does both at once, so its address, timers and listeners start fresh with the current connections. Runs opens its runs with every step's result, Resubmit and Cancel run; Versions deploys an earlier version; Tuning sets how the Sutra runs (below); Package history rolls the project back to an earlier package.
  • Traceability (View permission): every project you may see with its runs by outcome (done, failed, cancelled, open) over the last hour to 90 days. Open a project for its Sutras, deployed or not, with their ids, success rate, last run and last failure; open a Sutra for its runs. Find a run takes a run id (or its first characters), who started it, or a value anywhere in the data it started with, such as an order number. A run shows its ids (run, Sutra, project, each with Copy), who started it, what it started with, every step with its status, try, time, engine, error and full input and output (opened on request), its reply and log, and the runs it called or was called by (Call Sutra), each a click away. Download saves the whole run as JSON. Started by is a person (their account, for Run in the designer or Admin Console), an API client (the security policy's method and the caller it names: the token's subject, the API key's name or the user, with the address and gateway app; anonymous where the route has no policy), the system (a timer, listener, channel or alert), or another run. Runs from before 2.1.0 show only the kind of starter. What a step's data shows follows the Sutra's Step data tuning: all, only for failed runs, or none.
  • Approvals: what waits for a person and for whom (roles, accounts, progress, due time), with a button to open the Approval Center, where the approvers decide.
  • Releases: deploy a release zip (or .sutra package): choose the file, see its Sutras, the secrets present or missing on this server, where it was built from and its deployment config, change the project or give another config, then Deploy. Below, every project's current package with its history: Roll back, or Deploy again for any earlier one. This is how a production server receives Sutras.
  • Engines: the cluster's name, and every engine sharing the database: its name, alive or silent, leader, steps running, heartbeat, Node memory and May lead. Rename gives an engine a name people read; the cluster name is changed at the top (sutra engines cluster-name "Shop cluster"). Turning May lead off keeps an engine from leading (sutra engines lead <engine> --no); at least one engine must be allowed. Drain and stop asks one engine to finish its steps, hand the rest to the others and stop; your service manager starts it again. Delete old runs now runs housekeeping at once. Tuning on the same page sets engine values (below).

The Console panel and commands for every action

Console in the top bar opens a panel with every action taken in this browser tab: what was done, whether it worked, how long it took, and the server's answer. Each entry also shows the same action as a command, for Windows PowerShell and for Linux and macOS shells: the sutra command and the HTTP call (Invoke-RestMethod or curl). Every confirmation has Run it from a shell instead with the same commands, so an action can be scripted, put in a runbook, or tried again from a shell when the console is not at hand. Commands read the server address and token from SUTRA_SERVER and SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKEN; use a system account's API token. Passwords never appear in commands: they read NEW_PASSWORD from the environment.

sutra sutras list
sutra sutras restart "Order lookup API" --project "Orders"
sutra runs list --status failed
sutra runs resubmit 3f2c...
sutra approvals approve 42 --comment "checked"
sutra engines drain engine-2

Tuning

Tuning changes how deployed Sutras run, while they run. Every engine applies a change within a heartbeat, without a restart. Values set by environment variables stay the defaults, and an empty field returns to them.

Engine tuningWhat it does
Steps at onceSteps one engine runs at the same time. Set for all engines, or for one engine (a bigger machine, or 0 for a studio that should not run work).
Steps per run limitStops runs that take more steps, such as loops that never end.
Reply waitHow long REST, SOAP and MCP callers wait for a reply step.
Keep finished runs, Keep audit entriesDays before housekeeping deletes them.
Trace samplingShare of runs sent to the OpenTelemetry collector.
Sutra tuningWhat it does
Runs at onceMore runs wait as queued and start, oldest first, when one ends. Protects a slow partner system or a database.
PrioritySteps of higher priority Sutras are taken from the shared work queue first.
Run time limitRuns still open after this many minutes are cancelled with an error.
Retries, First retry afterFor steps whose own settings have no retries.
Step data in historyall, errors only (step data is kept only for runs that did not finish well), or none (for personal or bulky data).
Keep finished runsDays for this Sutra, instead of the engine setting.

Sutra tuning applies to every run of the deployed Sutra, whether its one starter is a REST or SOAP request, timer, file, mailbox, queue, MCP skill or channel, or it is invoked through the Run API. Test and debug runs from the designer are not tuned, and runs started by Call Sutra always start (they count toward the limit, but never wait behind their own caller). Sutra tuning stays when a new version is deployed. Tuned Sutras show tuned in Applications.

Alerts

The Overview shows open alerts, runs of the last day and gateway traffic as charts. Under Alerts:

  • Channels say where alerts go: email through any project's SMTP connection, a webhook (a JSON POST with event, text and alert; chat tools that read a text field show the message; optionally signed with X-Sutra-Signature from a vault secret), or a deployed Sutra that starts with the alert as its input, to open a ticket or call someone. Send a test tries a channel.
  • Alert rules say what to watch: failed runs (of one Sutra or any), slow runs, gateway error rate, gateway latency (p95), engines (one stopped beating, or fewer alive than needed), work waiting in the queue too long, approvals waiting too long, the gateway certificate ending soon, listeners in error. Each rule has a severity (warning or critical), channels, whether to tell when it resolves, and reminders every few minutes while nobody acknowledged it. Check now shows what the rule finds at this moment.
  • Alerts lists what is open, newest first, and the history. The cluster leader checks every rule every 30 seconds, so a cluster alerts once; one alert per rule stays open until its condition clears. Acknowledge says someone is on it and stops reminders; Resolve closes it by hand. Each alert shows what was sent where, and whether it arrived.
sutra alerts                 (open alerts; exit code 1 while a critical alert is firing)
sutra alerts ack <id>
sutra alerts test "Operations team"

Gateway: apps, keys, plans, firewall, traffic

  • Apps and keys: an app is a consumer of your APIs (a partner, a mobile app, a team) with scopes such as orders:read and a plan. Create keys for it; each is shown once. Callers send a key in X-API-Key, or exchange it for an access token at POST /oauth/token on the gateway (client credentials: the app id and a key). Disabling an app or revoking a key refuses its calls at once.
  • To protect a service with apps, give its API security policy the authentication apps and the Required scopes.
  • Plans: requests per minute, hour and day and a monthly quota. All engines count together; over a limit the caller gets 429 with Retry-After, and every answer carries X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining.
  • Firewall: addresses or ranges the whole gateway allows or denies.
  • Traffic: requests over time (answered, refused, errors), latency p50/p95/p99, the busiest and slowest services, apps, status codes, and the request log with every request's caller, time and error.
  • APIs: what is served, with its policy; OpenAPI for the REST services, and the options to publish it at /openapi.json and to keep the request log.
sutra gateway plan set Partner --per-minute 120 --per-day 50000
sutra gateway app add "Acme shop" --scopes "orders:read" --plan Partner
sutra gateway key create "Acme shop" --name production --expires-days 365
sutra gateway stats --period 24h

Users, system accounts and roles

  • Users are people. An administrator adds them with a first password (Generate makes a strong one); by default they choose their own at the first sign-in. Five wrong passwords lock an account for 15 minutes; Unlock ends it sooner. Disable ends the person's sessions at once and keeps everything; Sign out everywhere ends sessions only.
  • System accounts are for engines, CI pipelines and API callers. They do not sign in to the designer. They get API tokens for the admin API, shown once and stored only as a hash, with an expiry and a Revoke button. A system account with a password can call gateway services whose API security policy accepts system accounts.
  • Roles are sets of permissions. A role is granted for all projects or for one project, and an account can hold several. Built-in roles: Administrator, Developer, Deployer, Operator, Approver, Viewer and API caller. New role combines permissions differently.
PermissionAllows
ViewSee the project, its Sutras, connections, runs and logs.
DesignEdit Sutras, schemas and project settings; test and debug runs.
ConnectionsAdd and change connections and API security policies.
DeployDeploy and undeploy Sutras, deploy packages, roll back, edit the deployment config.
OperateStart, stop, cancel and resubmit; clear runtime variable values.
ApproveDecide approvals.
Call servicesSystem accounts: call the project's gateway services with Basic sign-in.
Secrets, Engines, Gateway, Server settings, Users and roles, Audit, Alerts (channels, rules, acknowledging)Server permissions: they only come with a grant on all projects.
Always one administrator

Nobody can disable or delete their own account, and the last active administrator cannot lose the role.

Audit log

Every change, sign-in and refused request is recorded with who, when, from which address, what and the result, and with where it happened:

  • Where: the server (production, test or development, from SUTRA_ENVIRONMENT) and the engine, and whether it was a designer test run or a deployed Sutra.
  • Project and Sutra: name and id. The names are kept with the entry, so a renamed or deleted Sutra still reads as it was.

Filter by server, project, Sutra (choose the project first), person, result, words and dates; Export CSV saves what the filters show, with all these columns. Passwords, secret values and tokens are never recorded. Entries recorded before this version show no server.

Audit retention and clearing

The Retention card at the top of the Audit page shows how many entries there are, the oldest, and when the log was last cleared and by whom. With the Audit settings and clearing permission (Administrators have it):

  • Keep entries (days): housekeeping deletes older entries; 0 keeps everything. The default is SUTRA_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS (365).
  • Delete older entries now, Clear before a date, or Clear all, each after a confirmation.

Clearing is recorded as an entry of its own (who, what, how many), so the log always shows that it was cleared. From a shell: sutra audit retention 180, sutra audit clear --before 2026-01-01.

Server

Runtime: script activities (Python, PowerShell, programs) and release activities, off until an administrator allows them, and the interpreters found. Gateway & TLS: the gateway's ports and certificate, your own or from Let's Encrypt. Database: the database in use and the move to PostgreSQL (Moving to PostgreSQL).

The first administrator of a headless engine

A headless engine has no first-start page, so nobody who reaches it can claim it. Add the first administrator on the server, then sign in at /admin:

sutra user add admin --role administrator --password-from-env ADMIN_PASSWORD
sutra user add ci-orders --system --role deployer --project "Orders"
sutra user list

Security and connections

15. Secrets and studio security

Single sign-on (OpenID Connect or SAML 2.0)

People can sign in to the designer, Admin Console and Approval Center with an OpenID Connect or SAML 2.0 identity provider (Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Keycloak, Google, Auth0 and compatible providers). Password sign-in stays available, so an administrator can always get in.

  1. Open Admin Console → Users → Single sign-on and choose OpenID Connect or SAML 2.0. Register the callback address shown there, such as https://sutra.example.com/api/auth/sso/callback. Behind a proxy, set SUTRA_PUBLIC_URL so it is the public address people use.
  2. For OpenID Connect, register a web application using the authorization-code flow, put its client secret in the vault, then enter the issuer, client id, secret name and claims. Ask the provider to include the person's groups in the ID token.
  3. For SAML, register SutraFlow as a service provider using the HTTP-POST response binding. Enter the identity-provider Redirect SSO address, the service-provider entity id/audience, the IdP issuer and its signing certificate. Choose the assertion attributes for username and groups, or use NameID as the username.
  4. Map groups to roles: sutra-admins to Administrator on all projects, shop-team to Operator on the Shop project. At every sign-in a person's roles become those of their groups.
  5. Choose Create accounts (people get an account at their first sign-in) and, only when the provider controls usernames, Link existing accounts.
  6. Turn on Offer single sign-on. The sign-in pages show Sign in with your provider.

OpenID Connect uses the authorization-code flow with PKCE, state and nonce; the ID token's signature, issuer, audience and expiry are checked against the provider's published keys. SAML responses must carry a trusted signature and a single assertion bound to the one-time sign-in request, callback address, entity id, issuer and validity period. The one-time state is stored briefly in the shared database, and a signed short-lived cookie proves that the same browser or API client started the sign-in. A browserless client follows the same two requests: retain the sutra_sso cookie from /api/auth/sso/start and send it with the callback. A person is recognised by the provider subject or SAML NameID, so a renamed account stays the same person. Sign-ins with either protocol are in the audit log.

The vault and sessions

  • Passwords, keys and tokens live in the vault (Resources → Secrets), encrypted with AES-256-GCM. Settings hold the secret's name.
  • Secret values are never returned by the API. A secret used in a step is masked in stored outputs and logs.
  • The studio listens on 127.0.0.1 by default. Sessions are HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookies; every change needs a request header that browsers cannot forge across sites; repeated failed sign-ins are slowed down.

16. Connections on production servers

A project deployed to another server brings its connections, but never their passwords, keys or tokens. Each server signs in on its own, so test and production can use different accounts, and a package can go to production without anyone copying a secret.

CredentialHow production gets it
Passwords, keys, client secrets, access tokensFields of type secret hold only a name. The package lists the names (README, Releases check); put the values in the production vault with sutra secret set NAME --from-env NAME from the pipeline's secret store, or Resources > Secrets. A missing secret stops the deploy before anything changes.
Other settings (hosts, factory, workspace, folders)The deployment config of that environment; any value may read ${env:NAME}.
Azure identitiesBest: a managed identity on the production server (no secret). Else a service principal per environment, its secret in that server's vault.
OAuth accounts (Google, YouTube, Twitch, Dropbox, Facebook, Microsoft)One of: sutra connect (below); a refresh token secret on the connection; or Connect account in that server's studio. Tokens are encrypted with that server's master key and never leave it.

Setting up each provider's app (client ID, secret, redirect address, scopes) and signing in, step by step: OAuth connections step by step.

sutra connect

sutra connect "Sample Google (Drive and YouTube)" --project Media --server https://prod-engine:4800 --token $TOKEN

It prints the sign-in address for that server; open it in a browser, sign in to the account, and the command reports when the server has its tokens. The OAuth app must list that server's redirect address (shown by the command). Headless engines accept it too.

A refresh token secret

When no person may sign in on production, give the OAuth connection a Refresh token (secret): a refresh token of the account, kept as a secret on that server and set by the pipeline. The server signs in with it on first use. Get the refresh token once with the provider's tools (for Google, the OAuth Playground with your own client), store it in your secret manager, and rotate it like any other secret.

Certificates and private keys

Every connection and security policy that needs a certificate or a key (databases, Kafka, RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, MongoDB, SFTP, outbound TLS and WS-Security, inbound JWT, X.509 and SAML) has one setting for each, and that setting can be any of:

GiveExampleGood for
A file on the serverC:\certs\aiven\ca.pem, \\server\certs\ca.pem, /etc/ssl/sutraflow/ca.pem, ~/certs/ca.pem, or relative to the data folderServers where certificates are files managed by the operating system or a tool. Renew by replacing the file.
A path with a variable{{ev.CERTS}}\ca.pem or {{ev.CERTS}}/ca.pemOne folder per server or environment, set once as an engine property.
A Certificate property{{gv.KAFKA_CA}}: a project or engine property of type certificate holding the PEM text or a file pathContainers and test servers: paste the certificate once; every connection that names it follows a change.
A Private key property{{gv.KAFKA_KEY}}: type private key, kept encrypted in the vault like a Secret, never shown againClient keys when no key file can be placed on the server.

Windows and Linux paths both work; on Linux and macOS a backslash is read as a folder separator too, so a deployment config written on Windows (certs\ca.pem) works unchanged. A key file must be readable only by the account SutraFlow runs as. A key passphrase is always a Secret property. Connections made before 2.1.1 keep the PEM text pasted into them. Passwords and other secrets are chosen from Secret properties only; their values are entered under Configuration, Project variables (engine properties by administrators in the Admin Console), never in the connection.

Good practice

Separate accounts per environment: a test YouTube channel, a test factory, a test workspace.
Least rights: only the scopes and roles the Sutras use.
Test connection after every deploy, from the Admin Console or the Releases check.

Releases on servers

17. Receiving releases on a server

Designers build releases (User Guide: Releases); administrators put them on test and production servers. A release moves a whole project unchanged: the same file goes from test to UAT to production, and each server keeps its own deployment config and its own secrets.

In a release zipHolds
package.sutraEvery Sutra at its version, connections and API policies with secret names only, schemas, project variables and logging, with a checksum
deployment-config.jsonWhat differs per server, to fill in: connection settings, project variables, logging; values may read ${env:NAME}
README.txt, documentation.htmlSutras and their addresses, the secrets the server needs, where it was built from, and the deploy and rollback commands
files/Documents and templates the project needs

Prepare the server

  1. Secrets: put every name the README lists in this server's vault: sutra secret set ORDERS_DB --from-env ORDERS_DB, or Admin Console. A missing secret stops the deploy before anything changes.
  2. Deployment config: hosts, folders and users of this server; keep one file per environment, with ${env:...} for values from the server's environment.
  3. Access: a system account with the Deploy permission on the project (Admin Console, System accounts) and an API token for the pipeline.

Deploy

  • Admin Console, Releases: choose the zip; read its check (Sutras and addresses, secrets present or missing, where it was built from, its config and files); change the project name or give another config; Deploy. Below, every project's package history with Roll back and Deploy again.
  • Command line: sutra check release.zip, then sutra deploy release.zip [--config prod.json], with --server https://engine:4800 --token $TOKEN for a remote server. sutra history, sutra rollback --project "Orders" [--to <id>].
  • Headless engines deploy the packages in SUTRA_DEPLOY_DIR at start, in file-name order; a package already deployed is skipped, and one that cannot be deployed stops the start, so a bad release never serves half-deployed.

Before anything changes the package is checked: checksum, activities this server knows, every secret present, and no REST or SOAP path or MCP skill already served by another project. Then everything is matched by name: the project (made when missing), schemas, connections, Sutras. Changed Sutras get a new version; unchanged ones are left alone, so deploying the same package twice changes nothing; Sutras of the project not in the package are undeployed (kept, not deleted) unless keep others. Every deployment is recorded with who deployed it, and a rollback is itself a deployment.

Production servers

A server with SUTRA_ENVIRONMENT=production refuses Deploy from the designer: it gets Sutras only from releases. sutra test release.zip runs every Sutra of a package with its test data in a throw-away server before it goes anywhere.

The first administrator of a headless engine

A headless engine has no first-start page, so nobody who reaches it can claim it. The installer makes the administrator; on an engine installed by hand, add one on the server, then sign in at /admin:

sutra user add admin --role administrator --password-from-env ADMIN_PASSWORD
sutra user add ci-orders --system --role deployer --project "Orders"
sutra token create ci-orders --name github --expires-days 90
Good practice

Promote the same zip from UAT to production; never rebuild it for production.
Give each environment its own system account and token, with Deploy on the project only.
Keep the zips: they are the record of what went live, and the way back.

Reference and troubleshooting

18. Command reference

SutraFlow has two command line tools. Both lists below are read from the tools themselves when this guide is built, so they always match the version you have; sutraflow help and sutra help print the same.

  • sutraflow runs SutraFlow on this machine: install, start, stop, status, logs, Docker. Windows: bin\sutraflow.cmd; Linux and macOS: bin/sutraflow; sutraflow after npm install -g.
  • sutra works with what is in SutraFlow: packages and releases, users, secrets, deployed Sutras, runs, approvals, engines, alerts and the gateway. It works on the data folder directly, or on a running server with --server and --token. sutraflow cli <command> runs it against the local studio, already signed in; on its own it is npm run sutra -- <command> or sutra after npm install -g.

sutraflow: running SutraFlow

CommandWhat it does
sutraflow install [--port 4790] [--no-open] [--reset]The web installer: administrator, database (with a connection test), ports, cluster; or an upgrade of an installation from 2.1.0 on. It opens in the browser and answers on this machine only. --reset unlocks it after an install.
sutraflow install --config install.json [--dry-run]
sutraflow upgrade --config upgrade.json [--dry-run]The same without a browser, from a JSON file (passwords as {"env": "NAME"} or {"file": "path"}); --dry-run prints the plan. See docs/install-example.json.
sutraflow setup [--ports]Installs the packages and builds SutraFlow (from a source folder), and makes sutraflow.env and the local admin token; asks for the ports when it makes sutraflow.env (or with --ports), checking that each is free.
sutraflow start [engine] [--foreground]Starts the studio (designer, Admin Console, engine and gateway), or a headless engine beside it on the same database. In the background unless --foreground; its output goes to <data>/logs/<name>.out.log.
sutraflow stop [engine|all] [--force]Stops gracefully: no new work, running steps finish (up to 30 s). --force ends the process when it does not stop in time.
sutraflow restart [engine]Stops, then starts.
sutraflow statusStudio and engine: running or not, ready, addresses, database.
sutraflow logs [engine] [--follow]The last lines of the output log.
sutraflow open [designer|admin|guide|admin-guide|architecture]Opens the page in the browser.
sutraflow cli <sutra command ...>The sutra command, pointed at this studio with the local admin token, for example: sutraflow cli sutras list
sutraflow db info | db copy --to <postgres://...> [--replace]Which database is in use; copies the data to PostgreSQL (stop first). To move to PostgreSQL in one go (stop, copy, switch, start, check): tools/migrate-to-postgres, or Admin Console > Database > Migrate now.
sutraflow serviceHow to start SutraFlow with the machine (systemd unit or Windows task).
sutraflow docker up | down | status | logs [service] | buildThe studio and an engine in Docker (docker-compose.yml).
sutraflow docker cluster up | down | status | logsPostgreSQL, a studio and two engines (docker-compose.cluster.yml).
sutraflow versionThe SutraFlow version.

Settings: sutraflow.env in the SutraFlow folder (ports, data folder, SUTRA_DB, Node path); SUTRAFLOW_ENV names another file.

sutra: releases, people and operations

CommandWhat it does
Releases
sutra package --project <name> [--version 1.0.0] [--note text] [--sutras "A,B"] [--zip] [--out file]Builds a package of a project: every deployed Sutra at its deployed version. With --zip or an --out ending in .zip, a release zip: the package, a deployment config to fill in for the target (connections, project variables, secrets needed) and a README.
sutra package --from-git <repository address | folder> [--ref <tag|branch|commit>] [--version 1.0.0] [--note text] [--sutras "A,B"] [--out release.zip]Builds a release zip from the project's files in Git, with no server or database, for CI/CD pipelines. Every Sutra in the repository (or the chosen ones) is deployed by it. A private repository reads its token from SUTRA_GIT_TOKEN (login SUTRA_GIT_LOGIN).
sutra check <release.zip | file.sutra> [--project <name>]Checks a package against a server: activities, secrets, addresses in use.
sutra deploy <release.zip | file.sutra> [--project <name>] [--config deployment-config.json] [--keep-others]Deploys a package with its deployment config (the zip's own, or --config); Sutras of the project not in it are undeployed unless --keep-others.
sutra test <release.zip | file.sutra> [--skip "A,B"] [--secret NAME=value ...] [--secrets-from-env]Installs the package in a throw-away server and runs every Sutra with its test data.
sutra history --project <name>Deployments of packages to a project.
sutra doc (--project <name> [--sutra <name>] | <release.zip | file.sutra>) [--format html|md] [--out file]Documentation made from the Sutras and their step descriptions: what starts each Sutra, its steps in order with their settings, connections and variables.
sutra rollback --project <name> [--to <id>]Deploys the package before the current one, or the deployment with that id.
Server, data and people
sutra statusServer health, readiness and engines.
sutra connect <connection> --project <name> [--wait-minutes 10]Signs in an OAuth connection (Google, YouTube, Twitch, ...) on a server without the studio: prints the sign-in address, and waits until the account is connected. The server's /api/oauth/callback address must be a redirect address of the OAuth app. Needs --server.
sutra python [--set <path to python> | --clear]Which Python runs Python steps on the server; --set chooses an interpreter.
sutra secret set <NAME> (--value <v> | --from-env <VAR>)Saves a secret in the vault (encrypted); Sutras and connections use it by name.
sutra db copy --to <postgres://user:pass@host/db | file.db> [--replace]Copies this server's data (SUTRA_DATA_DIR or SUTRA_DB) to another database, for example from SQLite to PostgreSQL. A missing PostgreSQL database is created. Stop the server first; then start it with SUTRA_DB set to the new address and the same master key.
sutra db infoWhich database the server uses, and its row counts.
sutra db migrate [--url <postgres://...>] [--replace] [--write-env <sutraflow.env>]Copies this server's SQLite data to the PostgreSQL connection saved on the Admin Console's Database page (or --url), checks every table arrived, and with --write-env points that settings file at PostgreSQL (old file kept). Stop the server first; the script tools/migrate-to-postgres does the whole move, stop and start included.
sutra user add <name> [--role administrator] [--project <name>] [--system] [--display "Name"] [--email e] [--password <p> | --password-from-env <VAR>] [--keep-password]Adds a person (or a system account) with a role for all projects or one project. People choose a new password at their first sign-in unless --keep-password. This is how a headless engine gets its first administrator.
sutra user listPeople and system accounts with their roles.
sutra user password <name> (--password <p> | --password-from-env <VAR>)Sets a new password; the person chooses their own at the next sign-in.
sutra user disable | enable | unlock | sign-out | delete <name>Blocks or allows sign-in, clears a lock after wrong passwords, ends all sessions, or deletes.
Operating deployed Sutras (the same actions as the Admin Console; need --server)
sutra sutras list [--project <name>]Deployed Sutras with their state and runs of the last 24 hours.
sutra sutras start | stop | restart <sutra> --project <name>Starts or stops a deployed Sutra's triggers; restart does both.
sutra sutras deploy <sutra> --project <name> --version <n>Deploys a published version of a Sutra (an earlier one to go back).
sutra sutras tune <sutra> --project <name> [--max-runs n] [--priority n] [--run-timeout-min n] [--retries n] [--retry-delay-ms n] [--step-data all|errors-only|none] [--retention-days n] [--execution durable|in-memory]Tuning of one Sutra: runs at a time, priority, time limit, retries, what runs keep and how long, and whether it runs durable or in memory.
sutra runs list [--sutra <name> --project <name>] [--status failed] [--limit 50]Recent runs, newest first.
sutra runs show | resubmit | cancel <run id>One run step by step; runs it again from its failed steps; or cancels it.
sutra approvals list | approve <id> [--comment text] | reject <id> [--comment text]Steps waiting for a person, and the decision on one.
sutra engines list | drain <engine> | restart <engine> | housekeepingEngines of the cluster; stops one gracefully; deletes runs and audit entries past retention.
sutra engines lead <engine> --yes|--no | cluster-name <name>Whether an engine may lead (the leader is elected among those that may), and the cluster's name.
sutra engines tune [--engine <id>] [--workers n] [--max-steps n] [--reply-timeout-ms n] [--retention-days n] [--audit-retention-days n] [--trace-sampling 0..1] [--memory-workers n] [--poll-ms n] [--settings-refresh-ms n] [--memory-mb n]Engine tuning, for every engine or one: workers, limits, retention, trace sampling, queue check; Node memory (MB, applies at restart: sutra engines restart <engine>).
sutra engines machineThe cores and memory of the machine the engine runs on (read when it starts), and the settings recommended for it. Every engine reads its own machine, so each install gets its own advice.
sutra engines name <engine id> <display name>The name people see for an engine in the Admin Console ("" = its id). The id stays the same.
sutra memory list [--project <name>] | rows <table> --project <name> [--find text] [--offset n] [--limit 50]Memory tables with their settings and figures on this engine, and their rows a page at a time.
sutra memory reload | clear <table> --project <name>Loads a memory table again from its source on every engine (hot reload), or empties it.
sutra memory set <table> --project <name> --row '{"code":"EUR","rate":1.08}' [--key EUR] | remove <table> --project <name> --key EURChanges one value by hand, or removes it.
sutra token create <system account> [--name text] [--expires-days n] | list <account> | revoke <account> <id>API tokens of a system account, for scripts and pipelines.
sutra audit [--actor name] [--outcome ok|failed|denied] [--from 2026-10-01] [--csv]Who did what, when, and with what outcome.
sutra audit retention [<days>]How long audit entries are kept; with a number, sets it (0 = keep everything).
sutra audit clear --before 2026-10-01 | --older | --allClears audit entries before a date, older than the retention, or all; the clearing is recorded.
Alerts (need --server)
sutra alerts [list | history] | ack <id> | resolve <id> | check | rules | channels | test <channel>Open and past alerts, acknowledging and resolving them, checking now, the rules and channels, and a test message to a channel.
Gateway (apps, keys, plans, firewall, traffic; need --server)
sutra gateway apps | plans | stats [--period 1h|24h|7d|30d] | log [--status errors|refused|ok] [--limit n]Apps, plans, traffic statistics and the request log.
sutra gateway app add <name> [--scopes "orders:read orders:write"] [--plan <name>] [--contact text]Adds an app that calls your APIs, with its scopes and plan.
sutra gateway app disable | enable | delete <name>Blocks, allows or deletes an app.
sutra gateway key create <app> [--name text] [--expires-days n] | key revoke <app> <key id>Makes an API key for an app (shown once) or revokes one.
sutra gateway plan set <name> [--per-minute n] [--per-hour n] [--per-day n] [--per-month n] | plan delete <name>Request limits of a plan.
sutra gateway firewall [--allow "10.0.0.0/8,192.168.1.5"] [--deny "203.0.113.9"]Addresses allowed and refused; with no options, shows them.
sutra gateway openapiOpenAPI of the deployed services (JSON).

Remote: --server <url> --token <token> (or SUTRA_SERVER, SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKEN). The token is a system account's API token (limited to its roles) or the server's SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKEN.

Exit code 0 = success, 1 = failure, 2 = wrong usage.

Examples

sutraflow setup                               install and build
sutraflow start                               the studio, in the background
sutraflow start engine                        a second engine on the same database
sutraflow status                              what runs, where, on which database
sutraflow cli sutras list                     deployed Sutras with their runs today
sutraflow cli runs list --status failed       failed runs
sutraflow cli user add meera --role developer --password-from-env NEW_PASSWORD
sutraflow db copy --to postgres://postgres@127.0.0.1:5432/sutraflow
sutraflow stop all                            graceful: running steps finish first
sutra package --project Shop --version 1.4.0 --out shop-1.4.0.sutra
sutra deploy shop-1.4.0.sutra --server https://prod:4800 --token $SUTRA_TOKEN
Guidelines

Run sutraflow stop before db copy, so nothing changes while the data is copied.
Give scripts a system account and its API token (sutra user add --system, sutra token create) rather than the local admin token.

19. Troubleshooting servers

What you seeWhat to do
The installer says SutraFlow is already installed in this folderIt locked itself after the install (data/install.lock). To bring another installation up to this version, choose Upgrade; to install again here, sutraflow install --reset first.
Test connection in the installer: pgvector is not installedInstall pgvector on the PostgreSQL server (Development machines for Laragon and Linux), or choose Continue without pgvector when no knowledge base will be kept in PostgreSQL.
A port is in useAnother program, or another SutraFlow, listens there. Use the suggested free port; sutraflow status shows what each SutraFlow process uses.
The upgrade stopped at Program files freeA program holds files of the installation without sharing; the message names the files and, on Windows, the process (id and name). Stop that program (a SutraFlow process started by hand, an editor with a file open, an indexer) or let it finish, and run the upgrade again: nothing was changed. Web servers, terminals and Explorer windows in the folder do not need closing.
The upgrade stopped at BackupThe dump could not be read back, or the backup folder is full: nothing was changed. Free space, or give another backup folder.
The upgrade failed and put the previous version backThe page and data/logs/installer.log name the step and the reason; the backup is in backups/<version>-<time>. Fix the cause and run the upgrade again.
"The database was not restored" after a failed upgradeA process still held its tables (an engine on another machine). Stop every engine of the cluster and restore the dump from the backup by hand: pg_restore --clean --if-exists -d <database> database.dump.
An engine does not start; the log ends with the Node.js versionThat line only ends a crash: read the error above it in <data>/logs/<name>.out.log. A Node memory size too large for the machine is one cause; lower it in sutraflow.env (STUDIO_MEMORY_MB, ENGINE_MEMORY_MB).
Timers and listeners stopped in a clusterNo engine that may lead is alive. Admin Console, Engines shows the leader and never leads; allow another engine to lead, or start one that may.
Secrets cannot be read after a move or a restoreThe master key differs. Use the same data/master.key (or SUTRA_MASTER_KEY) as the server the data came from.
Callers get 403 behind a proxyThe proxy forwards to the gateway's HTTP port while the policy requires HTTPS: forward to the HTTPS port (Planning a server).
Let's Encrypt failsPort 80 on the domain must reach the gateway's HTTP port.
